sections.content: You know the *repetición* and the rhetorical question from B2 Unit 36: devices that make a point stick. An editorial uses them in a fixed order of effect. A rhetorical question puts the other side on the defensive and makes the reader answer in their head. A list of three gives a claim rhythm and weight. A closing call asks the reader or the authorities to act, and it comes last, because nothing should follow it. For the call, use *Que* + subjunctive (wishes, as in A2 Unit 27) or *Es hora de* + infinitive. One device is enough for a paragraph. Three in a row sound like a speech.

sections.title: Three moves
rows: How long are we going to wait? (rhetorical question: no answer expected)
Queremos un centro más tranquilo, más limpio y más seguro.
We want a calmer, cleaner and safer centre. (list of three: the repeated *más* builds the rhythm)
May the council decide now. (closing call with que + subjunctive)

items.spanish: ¿Para quién es el centro de la ciudad: para el tráfico o para las personas?
items.english: Who is the centre of the city for: traffic or people?

items.spanish: Es una medida justa, necesaria y urgente.
items.english: It is a measure that is fair, necessary and urgent.

items.spanish: Que nadie se esconda tras el pretexto de que el cambio es difícil.
items.english: Let nobody hide behind the excuse that the change is difficult.

sections.content: English adds "isn't it?" to turn a statement into a question. Spanish does not need it: the question stands alone, with both signs (*¿…?*). In a list of three, keep the same shape for each item (three adjectives, or three *más* + adjective), and put *y* only before the last. Finish on the call. A closing hedge such as *quizá* takes the force out of it.
